opinion-1.title: The Great American Betrayal
lines: Deliberately deceiving voters at scale should be treated as a crime against self-government. It is a betrayal of the republic, because free elections assume that citizens can give informed consent. When false claims are pushed, amplified, and left standing long after the record has corrected them, that consent is poisoned.

Hannah Arendt named what is at stake. In The Origins of Totalitarianism (enlarged 2nd ed., 1958; the passage is from “Ideology and Terror,” first published in 1953) she wrote: “The ideal subject of totalitarian rule is not the convinced Nazi or the convinced Communist, but people for whom the distinction between fact and fiction (i.e., the reality of experience) and the distinction between true and false (i.e., the standards of thought) no longer exist.” In “Truth and Politics” (The New Yorker, 1967) she argued that factual truth is the ground political opinion stands on: “Freedom of opinion is a farce unless factual information is guaranteed and the facts themselves are not in dispute.” Factual truth, she wrote, “is always in danger of being maneuvered out of the world not only for a time but, potentially, forever.” In “Lying in Politics” (1971), reflecting on the Pentagon Papers, she found that the policy of lying was “chiefly if not exclusively destined for domestic consumption, for propaganda at home and especially for the purpose of deceiving Congress.” In a 1974 interview with Roger Errera, published in The New York Review of Books in 1978, she warned: “a people that no longer can believe anything cannot make up its mind. It is deprived not only of its capacity to act but also of its capacity to think and to judge.”

Current U.S. law protects much false speech. In United States v. Alvarez (2012) the Supreme Court struck down the Stolen Valor Act, and the plurality wrote that “falsity alone may not suffice to bring the speech outside the First Amendment.” Under New York Times Co. v. Sullivan (1964), a public official suing over a falsehood about official conduct must prove “actual malice”: that the statement was made “with knowledge that it was false or with reckless disregard of whether it was false or not.” This section is not a claim about what the courts already punish. It is an argument about what accountability should become: if a free people cannot tell fact from fiction, they cannot govern themselves.
more: Congress, which writes the rules for itself, has betrayed voters by refusing to police its own members' false statements. Cases in this record were pushed by sitting Representatives, Senators, Speakers, and party leaders in the House and Senate. The Speech or Debate Clause (art. I, § 6) protects legislative acts, but not everything a member does in public. In Gravel v. United States (1972) the Court held that a senator's private publication of the Pentagon Papers “was in no way essential to the deliberations of the Senate” and was not protected. In Hutchinson v. Proxmire (1979) it held that “neither the newsletters nor the press release was ‘essential to the deliberations of the Senate’”; the Clause did not shield them.

Even so, the House rarely uses its own discipline. Its historians list 6 expulsions and 29 censures in its entire history. On June 21, 2023, the House censured Rep. Adam Schiff over Russia-related claims (H. Res. 521), 213–209 with 6 present: every yea was Republican and every nay was Democrat. That is a rarely used tool applied along party lines, not a standing accuracy rule.

opinion-4.title: The same evidence for everyone
lines: In my opinion, the damage to the nation is universal, done by everyone holding a microphone, regardless of party or network. As Hannah Arendt warned, a people fed constant lies ends up not knowing what the truth is. That is why this site holds everyone to the same evidence.

Her words, from a 1974 interview with Roger Errera published in The New York Review of Books in 1978: “a people that no longer can believe anything cannot make up its mind. It is deprived not only of its capacity to act but also of its capacity to think and to judge.”
